what_its_for: Ethosuximide is used to control a type of seizure called absence seizures (also called petit mal seizures). These are brief episodes where a person may stare blankly, blink rapidly, or seem to 'zone out' for a few seconds. This medicine helps reduce how often these seizures happen.
how_to_take: Take ethosuximide by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. It comes as a capsule or a liquid syrup. You can take it with food or milk if it upsets your stomach. Swallow capsules whole. If you are using the liquid, use a measuring spoon or oral syringe to get the right dose — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Take this medicine at the same time(s) every day to keep it working well.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it until your seizures are controlled. For children 3 to 6 years old, the usual starting dose is 250 mg once a day. For children older than 6 and adults, the usual starting dose is 500 mg per day. Your doctor may adjust your dose every 4 to 7 days as needed. The typical effective dose ranges from 20 to 40 mg per kilogram of body weight per day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Missing doses can increase your risk of having seizures, so try to take your medicine at the same time every day.
storage: Store ethosuximide capsules and syrup at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine past its expiration date.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking ethosuximide, as it can increase dizziness and drowsiness. Be careful when driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be alert, especially when you first start the medicine. Avoid stopping this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause seizures to come back or get worse. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as some medicines can interact with ethosuximide.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: thoughts of hurting yourself or suicide, depression or unusual mood changes, a skin rash or blistering skin, fever with sore throat or mouth sores, unusual bruising or bleeding, signs of a serious allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing, loss of appetite or significant weight loss, or if your seizures get worse or you have a new type of seizure. Also call your doctor if you feel very dizzy, unsteady, or unusually drowsy.
when_it_works: Ethosuximide may start to reduce seizures within a few days, but it can take several weeks to find the right dose that works best for you. Do not stop taking it just because you feel better. Keep taking it every day as prescribed, even if you have not had a seizure in a long time. Your doctor will tell you if and when it is safe to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Ethosuximide may harm the baby, but untreated seizures can also be dangerous. Do not stop your medicine without talking to your doctor first. Breastfeeding: Ethosuximide passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits before breastfeeding. Children: This medicine is approved for children age 3 and older. Children should be monitored closely for mood changes or behavioral problems. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and drowsiness and should use this medicine with caution. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
